s: discriminating perception is a fundamental power of strong imagination (rather than a substitute for it)
q: her glorifying imagination is not an addition to the fundamental power of strong, discerning perception, but a cheaper substitute.

s: sanity consists in distinguishing external facts from imaginative revelations (for a seer after creative excitement)
q: that sanity of expectation which consists in distinguishing, as Dante does, between the _cose che son vere_ outside the individual mind, and the _non falsi errori_ which are the revelations of true imaginative power.

s: Callista has lax conception of common objects (as a habitual characteristic)
q: I find on listening to Callista's conversation, that she has a very lax conception even of common objects, and an equally lax memory of events.

s: the old heap of stones is a simple heap of stones (as actually perceived by Callista)
q: if she had taken a walk and seen an old heap of stones on her way, the account she would give on returning would include many pleasing particulars of her own invention, transforming the simple heap into an interesting castellated ruin.

s: Dante's triple vision causes forgetfulness of surroundings (during the vision)
q: after a triple vision which has made him forget his surroundings

s: Dante's triple vision contains ideal truth (distinguished from external facts after the vision)
q: He distinguishes the ideal truth of his entranced vision from the series of external facts to which his consciousness had returned.

s: Callista would transform the old heap of stones (in an embellished account)
q: the account she would give on returning would include many pleasing particulars of her own invention, transforming the simple heap into an interesting castellated ruin.

s: Callista has lax memory of events (as a habitual characteristic)
q: I find on listening to Callista's conversation, that she has a very lax conception even of common objects, and an equally lax memory of events.

s: Callista misrepresents facts (through habitual inaccuracy)
q: Her supposed imaginativeness is simply a very usual lack of discriminating perception, accompanied with a less usual activity of misrepresentation

s: Callista lacks discriminating perception (in her supposed imaginative ability)
q: Her supposed imaginativeness is simply a very usual lack of discriminating perception, accompanied with a less usual activity of misrepresentation

s: Callista could be a profuse writer (if her misrepresentation were more intense or circumstantially stimulated)
q: which, if it had been a little more intense, or had been stimulated by circumstance, might have made her a profuse writer unchecked by the troublesome need of veracity.

s: Dante is precise and homely in reproducing actual objects (while also being highly imaginative)
q: Witness Dante, who is at once the most precise and homely in his reproduction of actual objects, and the most soaringly at large in his imaginative combinations.

s: Dante distinguishes ideal vision from external facts (after returning from an entranced vision)
q: He distinguishes the ideal truth of his entranced vision from the series of external facts to which his consciousness had returned.

s: Dante is the strongest seer (when he sustains creative energy while retaining sane expectation)
q: But he is the strongest seer who can support the stress of creative energy and yet keep that sanity of expectation which consists in distinguishing, as Dante does, between the _cose che son vere_ outside the individual mind, and the _non falsi errori_ which are the revelations of true imaginative power.

s: the narrator is a bachelor (without domestic distractions)
q: I am a bachelor, without domestic distractions of any sort

s: self-knowledge and self-ignorance is limited by self-ignorance (which may be compensated by self-betrayal)
q: But the incompleteness which comes of self-ignorance may be compensated by self-betrayal.

s: the narrator's published humorous romance is a failed published work (humorous and unique in its kind)
q: as to intellectual contribution, my only published work was a failure, so that I am spoken of to inquiring beholders as "the author of a book you have probably not seen." (The work was a humorous romance, unique in its kind, and I am told is much tasted in a Cherokee translation, where the jokes are rendered with all the serious eloquence characteristic of the Red races.)

s: the narrator's published humorous romance is tasted in the Cherokee (in translation)
q: The work was a humorous romance, unique in its kind, and I am told is much tasted in a Cherokee translation

s: the narrator desires approbation, love, and social acceptance (permanently)
q: I find within me a permanent longing for approbation, sympathy, and love.

s: the narrator lacks social acceptance (in his personal lot)
q: Though continually in society, and caring about the joys and sorrows of my neighbours, I feel myself, so far as my personal lot is concerned, uncared for and alone.

s: the narrator has not received love (from the person he loves best)
q: the person I love best has never loved me, or known that I loved her

s: the narrator is not rich
q: It is to be borne in mind that I am not rich, have neither stud nor cellar, and no very high connections

s: the narrator has awkward feet (noticed by others as a physical disadvantage)
q: Then, in some quarters my awkward feet are against me, the length of my upper lip, and an inveterate way I have of walking with my head foremost and my chin projecting.

s: the narrator has a desire to be agreeable (innocent vanity)
q: This sort of reception to a man of affectionate disposition, who has also the innocent vanity of desiring to be agreeable

s: the narrator has a habit of self-observation (throughout life)
q: and have all my life been an attentive companion to myself

s: the narrator has a habit of attending to others' experience (as a corrective to self-partiality)
q: the habit of getting interested in the experience of others has been continually gathering strength

s: the narrator is regarded as a listener to personal outpouring (without becoming communicative in the same way)
q: he is evidently held capable of listening to all kinds of personal outpouring without the least disposition to become communicative in the same way

s: the narrator has established a habit of mind guarding against self-partiality (and promoting fair consideration of neighbours)
q: that I have at least succeeded in establishing a habit of mind which keeps watch against my self-partiality and promotes a fair consideration of what touches the feelings or the fortunes of my neighbours

s: sympathy and interest in others is hindered by my own dulness
q: if anything hindered my thought from rising to the force of passionately interested contemplation, or my poor pent-up pond of sensitiveness from widening into a beneficent river of sympathy, it was my own dulness

s: self-partiality and egoism is misleading and odious (whether dissatisfied or self-satisfied)
q: In my conscience I saw that the bias of personal discontent was just as misleading and odious as the bias of self-satisfaction.

s: self-partiality and egoism is a source of spiritual pride (when fed by egoistic consolation)
q: Fed in this way it is apt to become a monstrous spiritual pride, or a chuckling satisfaction that the final balance will not be against us but against those who now eclipse us.

s: the human race are liable to unconscious self-delusion (including failure to recognize their own absurdity)
q: It is in the nature of foolish reasoning to seem good to the foolish reasoner.

s: the human race cannot know their brothers merely as spectators (because shared possibilities enable recognition)
q: No man can know his brother simply as a spectator.

s: acquaintances possess knowledge of the narrator's powers and appearance (unknown to the narrator himself)
q: these others have certain items of knowledge about the extent of my powers and the figure I make with them, which in turn are secrets unguessed by me

s: the world contains a myriad of struggling lives (each life dear to itself)
q: And I had the mighty volume of the world before me. Nay, I had the struggling action of a myriad lives around me, each single life as dear to itself as mine to me.

s: the narrator remembers his own doings and sufferings (with unusually strong tenacity)
q: and in general remembering its doings and sufferings with a tenacity which is too apt to raise surprise if not disgust at the careless inaccuracy of my acquaintances

s: Delectable Mountain is a desired standpoint (for seeing things with reduced self-partiality)
q: The standing-ground worth striving after seemed to be some Delectable Mountain, whence I could see things in proportions as little as possible determined by that self-partiality

s: the narrator possesses secrets of inward experience (unknown even to intimate friends)
q: to whom I have never breathed those items of my inward experience which have chiefly shaped my life

s: the narrator is liable to being absurd without knowing it (as other human beings are)
q: I must still come under the common fatality of mankind and share the liability to be absurd without knowing that I am absurd

s: the narrator shares the weaknesses of human beings (despite discerning them in others)
q: the stronger to me is the proof that I share them

s: the narrator recognizes his own laughability (on unsuspected occasions)
q: I wince at the fact, but I am not ignorant of it, that I too am laughable on unsuspected occasions

s: the narrator is a fellow human being (not aloof from others)
q: Dear blunderers, I am one of you.

s: self-knowledge and self-ignorance includes incompleteness (in autobiography and self-description)
q: In all autobiography there is, nay, ought to be, an incompleteness which may have the effect of falsity.

s: the too ready writer is a writer
q: Why is there a different standard of judgment with regard to a writer who plays much the same part in literature as the excessive talker plays in what is traditionally called conversation?

s: Adrastus writes about the Colorado beetle (among chief current subjects)
q: from the tri-lingual inscriptions, or the Idea of the Infinite among the prehistoric Lapps, to the Colorado beetle and the grape disease in the south of France

s: Adrastus writes about the grape disease in the south of France (among chief current subjects)
q: from the tri-lingual inscriptions, or the Idea of the Infinite among the prehistoric Lapps, to the Colorado beetle and the grape disease in the south of France

s: Adrastus has breadth of mental range (as generally praised)
q: The busy Adrastus, whose professional engagements might seem more than enough for the nervous energy of one man, and who yet finds time to print essays on the chief current subjects, from the tri-lingual inscriptions, or the Idea of the Infinite among the prehistoric Lapps, to the Colorado beetle and the grape disease in the south of France, is generally praised if not admired for the breadth of his mental range and his gigantic powers of work.

s: Theron is excluded by Adrastus (from an advertised programme)
q: has been waiting anxiously from month to month to see whether his condensed exposition will find a place in the next advertised programme, but sees it, on the contrary, regularly excluded, and twice the space he asked for filled with the copious brew of Adrastus

s: Pepin is a general writer (serving the general reader)
q: He is already to be classed as a "general writer," corresponding to the comprehensive wants of the "general reader

s: Pepin raises some dust here below (while feeling himself powerful with the stars in their courses)
q: Like the astronomer in Rasselas, I swayed the universe in my consciousness without making any difference outside me; whereas Pepin, while feeling himself powerful with the stars in their courses, really raises some dust here below.

s: Pepin uses first impressions (as if they were deliberate opinions)
q: He is no longer in his spring-tide, but having been always busy he has been obliged to use his first impressions as if they were deliberate opinions

s: Pepin writes before having sufficient knowledge or belief (as a self-imposed necessity)
q: Pepin made for himself a necessity of writing (and getting printed) before he had considered whether he had the knowledge or belief that would furnish eligible matter.

s: Pepin has a fixed habit of writing (encouraged by early access to print)
q: Perhaps it is unfortunate for him that he early gained a hearing, or at least a place in print, and was thus encouraged in acquiring a fixed habit of writing, to the exclusion of any other bread-winning pursuit.

s: the too ready writer occupies literary space and time (exorbitantly)
q: but the exorbitant writer can occupy space and spread over it the more or less agreeable flavour of his mind in four "mediums" at once, and on subjects taken from the four winds.

s: Pepin loses accurate mental vision (through continual preoccupation with written judgments)
q: In this way he is irrevocably losing the faculty of accurate mental vision: having bound himself to express judgments which will satisfy some other demands than that of veracity, he has blunted his perceptions by continual preoccupation.

s: Pepin is more admirable than his written productions (in the personal relations of life)
q: He is much worthier and more admirable than his written productions, because the moral aspects exhibited in his writing are felt to be ridiculous or disgraceful in the personal relations of life.

s: Pepin's unwritten Roman romance is intended to present the splendours of the Roman Empire (at the culmination of its grandeur)
q: Pepin's romance was to present the splendours of the Roman Empire at the culmination of its grandeur, when decadence was spiritually but not visibly imminent

s: Pepin's unwritten Roman romance depicts the Roman Empire (at the culmination of its grandeur)
q: Pepin's romance was to present the splendours of the Roman Empire at the culmination of its grandeur, when decadence was spiritually but not visibly imminent

s: the public conscience sanctions the absence of scruple in writing and authorship (through lax and ill-informed standards)
q: In blaming Pepin's writing we are accusing the public conscience, which is so lax and ill informed on the momentous bearings of authorship that it sanctions the total absence of scruple in undertaking and prosecuting what should be the best warranted of vocations.

s: writing and authorship has internal consequences disease (when incessant and directed toward publication)
q: But Pepin is only a mild example of the fact that incessant writing with a view to printing carries internal consequences which have often the nature of disease.

s: writing and authorship requires veracity (as a vocation requiring scruple)
q: the public conscience, which is so lax and ill informed on the momentous bearings of authorship that it sanctions the total absence of scruple in undertaking and prosecuting what should be the best warranted of vocations.

s: veracity is a form of health (delicately guarded)
q: the power of seeing and reporting truly is a form of health that has to be delicately guarded

s: publicity and publication encourages the young (not readily, according to the narrator)
q: Such entertainment of scruple can hardly be expected from the young; but happily their readiness to mirror the universe anew for the rest of mankind is not encouraged by easy publicity.

s: the excessive talker is a conversation monopolist (in company)
q: One who talks too much, hindering the rest of the company from taking their turn, and apparently seeing no reason why they should not rather desire to know his opinion or experience in relation to all subjects, or at least to renounce the discussion of any topic where he can make no figure, has never been praised for this industrious monopoly of work which others would willingly have shared in.

s: the narrator has early astonishment at personal originality (in youth)
q: In the vivacious Pepin I have often seen the image of my early youth, when it seemed to me astonishing that the philosophers had left so many difficulties unsolved, and that so many great themes had raised no great poet to treat them.

s: the narrator maintains friendly relations with Pepin (despite criticizing his writing)
q: Hence I still accept friendly relations with Pepin, for he has much private amiability

s: conversation permits only one gathering at a time (for an excessive talker)
q: The excessive talker can only be in one gathering at a time

s: the four mediums are occupied by the too ready writer (simultaneously)
q: the exorbitant writer can occupy space and spread over it the more or less agreeable flavour of his mind in four "mediums" at once

s: the excessive talker excludes other writers (from contributing to conversation)
q: However various and brilliant his talk may be, we suspect him of impoverishing us by excluding the contributions of other minds, which attract our curiosity the more because he has shut them up in silence.

s: the excessive talker is a nuisance (to modest conversational participants)
q: On this ground even a modest person, without power or will to shine in the conversation, may easily find the predominating talker a nuisance

s: the narrator has monotony and narrowness (in personal identity)
q: There is monotony and narrowness already to spare in my own identity; what comes to me from without should be larger and more impartial than the judgment of any single interpreter.

s: Adrastus is a busy writer (professionally engaged and prolific)
q: The busy Adrastus, whose professional engagements might seem more than enough for the nervous energy of one man, and who yet finds time to print essays on the chief current subjects

s: Adrastus writes about the tri-lingual inscriptions (among chief current subjects)
q: from the tri-lingual inscriptions, or the Idea of the Infinite among the prehistoric Lapps, to the Colorado beetle and the grape disease in the south of France

s: Adrastus writes about the Idea of the Infinite among the prehistoric Lapps (among chief current subjects)
q: from the tri-lingual inscriptions, or the Idea of the Infinite among the prehistoric Lapps, to the Colorado beetle and the grape disease in the south of France

s: small authorship causes chronic ailments (moral and personal)
q: certain small chronic ailments that come of small authorship

s: Vorticella has magnified self-importance (a chronic moral ailment associated with her authorship)
q: giving her self-importance a troublesome kind of double incorporation which became oppressive to her acquaintances, and set up in herself one of those slight chronic forms of disease to which I have just referred

s: Vorticella possesses critical opinions album (for reviews of her book)
q: the opening pages in the elegantly bound album prepared by her for the reception of "critical opinions."

s: critical opinions album contains critical opinions (about Vorticella and her book)
q: every guest was allowed the privilege of reading what had been said of the authoress and her work

s: critical opinions album is located near the still more gorgeously bound work (on a special table in her drawing-room)
q: This ornamental volume lay on a special table in her drawing-room close to the still more gorgeously bound work of which it was the significant effect

s: The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix is a book (a thick octavo with notes and an appendix)
q: Her thick octavo--notes, appendix and all--was unflagging from beginning to end

s: The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix is reviewed by Pumpiter newspaper press (in all its organs of opinion)
q: Vorticella being the wife of an important townsman had naturally the satisfaction of seeing 'The Channel Islands' reviewed by all the organs of Pumpiter opinion

s: Pumpiter has Pumpiter newspaper press (with political and literary divisions)
q: had its own newspaper press, with the usual divisions of political partisanship and the usual varieties of literary

s: small authorship produces magnified self-importance (as a fungous disfiguration)
q: this sort of fungous disfiguration, which makes Self disagreeably larger

s: Vorticella is compared with Gregarina (as more tiresome because of her authorship)
q: This really made her more tiresome than Gregarina, whose distinction was that she had had cholera

s: Vorticella has chronic complaint (connected with The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix)
q: I understand that the chronic complaint of 'The Channel Islands' never left her.

s: Vorticella habitually lends The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix (to new acquaintances)
q: her chief interest in new acquaintances was the possibility of lending them her book

s: Vorticella habitually requests critical opinions album (that acquaintances read it)
q: requesting them to read her album of "critical opinions."

s: male vanity is denser texture (than female vanity)
q: while in women vanity lays by its small revenges as in a needle-case always at hand. The difference is in muscle and finger-tips, in traditional habits and mental perspective, rather than in the original appetite of vanity.

s: male vanity is more massive (than female vanity)
q: in the male it is of denser texture, less volatile, so that it less immediately informs you of its presence, but is more massive and capable of knocking you down if you come into collision with it

s: female vanity lays by small revenges (as in a needle-case always at hand)
q: while in women vanity lays by its small revenges as in a needle-case always at hand

s: authors is a miscellaneous class
q: Authors are so miscellaneous a class that their personified diseases, physical and moral, might include the whole procession of human disorders

s: female vanity is not superior to male vanity (in a fairly considered competition)
q: there is no need to admit that women would carry away the prize of vanity in a competition where differences of custom were fairly considered

s: authors has diseases including dyspepsia (among their personified diseases)
q: their personified diseases, physical and moral, might include the whole procession of human disorders, led by dyspepsia and ending in madness

s: Vorticella is a authoress (of one book)
q: Vorticella, who flourished in my youth not only as a portly lady walking in silk attire, but also as the authoress of a book entitled 'The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix.'

s: Vorticella is a portly lady (dressed in silk attire)
q: Vorticella, who flourished in my youth not only as a portly lady walking in silk attire

s: Vorticella wrote one book (no more than)
q: she wrote no more than one book

s: Vorticella lives in Pumpiter (a considerable provincial town)
q: She lived in the considerable provincial town of Pumpiter

s: Vorticella is married to Vorticella's husband (an important townsman)
q: Vorticella being the wife of an important townsman

s: Melissa judges Mr Barabbas (by his private sexual conduct)
q: Very different from Mr Barabbas, whose life, my husband tells me, is most objectionable, with actresses and that sort of thing.

s: Sir Gavial Mantrap is a commercial swindler (according to the narrator's judgment)
q: my opinion being that Sir Gavial was the more pernicious scoundrel of the two, since his name for virtue served as an effective part of a swindling apparatus

s: Sir Gavial Mantrap devises Mantrap's companies (to punish ignorance in people of small means)
q: other companies ingeniously devised by him for the punishment of ignorance in people of small means

s: Sir Gavial Mantrap cheats widows, spinsters, and hard-working fathers (of their savings through unscrupulous commercial activity)
q: the widows, spinsters, and hard-working fathers whom his unscrupulous haste to make himself rich has cheated of all their savings

s: Sir Gavial Mantrap possesses a wife's settlement of one or two hundred thousand in the consols (after his commercial disgrace)
q: the poor titled gentleman was actually reduced to live in comparative obscurity on his wife's settlement of one or two hundred thousand in the consols.

s: Sir Gavial Mantrap is a family man (according to Melissa)
q: Sir Gavial is an excellent family man--quite blameless there

s: Sir Gavial Mantrap is charitable at Tiptop (according to Melissa)
q: and so charitable round his place at Tiptop.

s: the States are concerned with constitution and prosperity (as the subject of political science)
q: political science or that which treats of the constitution and prosperity of States

s: Morality includes duties of man to man (in popular use)
q: Until we have altered our dictionaries and have found some other word than _morality_ to stand in popular use for the duties of man to man

s: society is a bond of societies
q: They are the original fountains of a sensibility to the claims of others, which is the bond of societies

s: the commonwealth is harmed by him (turning the channels of instruction into feeders of social and political disease)
q: let us pronounce him nevertheless flagrantly immoral, a root of hideous cancer in the commonwealth, turning the channels of instruction into feeders of social and political disease.

s: public spirit requires general welfare (as the governing consideration of conduct)
q: Do we desire to see public spirit penetrating all classes of the community and affecting every man's conduct, so that he shall make neither the saving of his soul nor any other private saving an excuse for indifference to the general welfare?

s: public spirit is harmed by ill-done work (when political activity replaces competent occupational work)
q: the sort of public spirit that scamps its bread-winning work, whether with the trowel, the pen, or the overseeing brain, that it may hurry to scenes of political or social agitation, would be as baleful a gift to our people as any malignant demon could devise.

s: ill-done work degrades the nation (through its effects on prosperity and commerce)
q: lax, make-shift work, from the high conspicuous kind to the average and obscure, is allowed to pass unstamped with the disgrace of immorality, though there is not a member of society who is not daily suffering from it materially and spiritually, and though it is the fatal cause that must degrade our national rank and our commerce

s: the relation between intellect and morality is presented as a radical opposition (as a popular absurdity)
q: the notion that there is a radical, irreconcilable opposition between intellect and morality.

s: religion is narrowed to ritual and spiritual transactions with God (in the criticized classification)
q: the other in certain ritual and spiritual transactions with God which can be carried on equally well side by side with the basest conduct towards men.

s: religious and ethical theory affects the mass of minds (through informal definitions of popular language)
q: The informal definitions of popular language are the only medium through which theory really affects the mass of minds even among the nominally educated

s: Morality is narrowed to sexual propriety (in popular speech)
q: the one of these consisting in not keeping mistresses (and perhaps not drinking too much)

s: Morals is a alias of Ethics (in public discussion)
q: Seeing that Morality and Morals under their _alias_ of Ethics are the subject of voluminous discussion

s: Morals is narrowed to private sexual conduct (in popular speech)
q: narrow use of the word _morals_, shutting out from its meaning half those actions of a man's life which tell momentously on the wellbeing of his fellow-citizens

s: Ethics is allied with political science (in the most famous ethical book and in college study)
q: the most famous book ever written on Ethics, and forming a chief study in our colleges, allies ethical with political science or that which treats of the constitution and prosperity of States

s: Melissa pities Sir Gavial Mantrap (because of his disgrace)
q: I found her disposed to speak pathetically of the disgrace which had fallen on Sir Gavial Mantrap

s: Melissa considers Sir Gavial Mantrap (a moral man despite his commercial conduct)
q: But Sir Gavial made a good use of his money, and he is a thoroughly _moral_ man.

s: Melissa defines morality as family respectability and local charity (in her judgment of Sir Gavial Mantrap)
q: Sir Gavial is an excellent family man--quite blameless there; and so charitable round his place at Tiptop.

s: Trost is a friend of the narrator
q: My friend Trost, who is no optimist as to the state of the universe hitherto, but is confident that at some future period within the duration of the solar system, ours will be the best of all possible worlds--a hope which I always honour as a sign of beneficent qualities--

s: the human race may be superseded by steely organisms
q: I get a little out of it, like an unfortunate savage too suddenly brought face to face with civilisation, and I exclaim-- "Am I already in the shadow of the Coming Race? and will the creatures who are to transcend and finally supersede us be steely organisms

s: machines are a extensions of the human organism (according to Trost)
q: They are simply extensions of the human organism, so to speak, limbs immeasurably more powerful, ever more subtle finger-tips, ever more mastery over the invisibly great and the invisibly small.

s: machines are extensions of the human organism (limbs immeasurably more powerful)
q: They are simply extensions of the human organism, so to speak, limbs immeasurably more powerful, ever more subtle finger-tips, ever more mastery over the invisibly great and the invisibly small.

s: machines may evolve self-supply (in the narrator's speculation)
q: how do I know that they may not be ultimately made to carry, or may not in themselves evolve, conditions of self-supply, self-repair, and reproduction

s: the Coming Race is a hypothetical successor species (composed of steely organisms in the narrator's vision)
q: will the creatures who are to transcend and finally supersede us be steely organisms, giving out the effluvia of the laboratory

s: consciousness is a stumbling of organisms (in the narrator's speculative premise)
q: if our consciousness is, as I have been given to understand, a mere stumbling of our organisms on their way to unconscious perfection

s: mechanical progress sets free human energy (for purportedly loftier purposes)
q: insisting so impressively on the quantity of energy which will thus be set free for loftier purposes

s: Trost expects machines to replace human labour (in the near future)
q: my friend Trost always tries to keep up my spirits under the sight of the extremely unpleasant and disfiguring work by which many of our fellow-creatures have to get their bread, with the assurance that "all this will soon be done by machinery."

s: national memories promote national greatness (by preserving and reviving collective identity)
q: That the preservation of national memories is an element and a means of national greatness, that their revival is a sign of reviving nationality

s: national consciousness is a living force of common sentiment (within a people)
q: It is this living force of sentiment in common which makes a national consciousness.

s: national consciousness raises man (above the brute)
q: the sense of corporate existence that raises man above the otherwise more respectable and innocent brute

s: Europe has excepted Jews (from ordinary rules of justice and mercy)
q: The European world has long been used to consider the Jews as altogether exceptional, and it has followed naturally enough that they have been excepted from the rules of justice and mercy, which are based on human likeness.

s: Greece is a modern nation (whose independence is attributed to the presence of ancient Greece in European consciousness)
q: That there is a free modern Greece is due--through all infiltration of other than Greek blood--to the presence of ancient Greece in the consciousness of European men

s: the Greeks possess ancient national memories (which helped inspire modern national independence)
q: That there is a free modern Greece is due--through all infiltration of other than Greek blood--to the presence of ancient Greece in the consciousness of European men

s: the English descend from the old English seamen (in the historian's account)
q: These seafaring, invading, self-asserting men were the English of old time, and were our fathers who did rough work by which we are profiting.

s: Trost holds humanity to be the nervous centre of mechanical processes (at the utmost development of those processes)
q: what you have heard me say is, that our race will and must act as a nervous centre to the utmost development of mechanical processes

s: the old English seamen accepted Christianity (with difficulty)
q: they had a decided objection to Christianity when it was first proposed to them

s: the title XVII. SHADOWS OF THE COMING RACE is a section title (for the discussion of mechanical succession to humanity)
q: XVII. SHADOWS OF THE COMING RACE.

s: the title XVIII. THE MODERN HEP! HEP! HEP! is a section title (for the discussion of nationality and the Jews)
q: XVIII. THE MODERN HEP! HEP! HEP!

s: Trost believes machines require human skill (for construction, supply, observation, and regulation)
q: Each new machine needs a new appliance of human skill to construct it, new devices to feed it with material, and often keener-edged faculties to note its registrations or performances. How then can machines supersede us?--they depend upon us. When we cease, they cease.

s: the narrator is a friend of Trost
q: My friend Trost

s: the narrator imagines a machine can reproduce itself by some process of fission or budding (after finding and assimilating material to supply its own waste)
q: What I would ask you is, to show me why, since each new invention casts a new light along the pathway of discovery, and each new combination or structure brings into play more conditions than its inventor foresaw, there should not at length be a machine of such high mechanical and chemical powers that it would find and assimilate the material to supply its own waste, and then by a further evolution of internal molecular movements reproduce itself by some process of fission or budding.

s: the narrator regards consciousness as an idle parasite (in a materialist account of organismic processes)
q: in truth it is an idle parasite on the grand sequence of things

s: the human race is a conscious organismic species (in the narrator's speculative argument)
